data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

A scientist noticed that South America and Africa look like puzzle pieces. Everyone laughed at him for fifty years. He was right — but for a reason he never figured out.

1. Read **The Man Who Was Laughed At** and watch how EVIDENCE piles up.
2. Learn the terms in the **Glossary**, then win the **Word Scramble**.
3. Follow **How We Figured It Out** — the timeline of the argument.
4. Sort the evidence in **What Kind of Boundary?**
5. Take the quiz — two questions ask what counts as EVIDENCE, not just what happened.
6. Fill in the **Cornell Notes** in your own words.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Earth Puzzle** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Explore: Reading a Coastline Like Wegener** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

The real lesson here is not about rocks. It is about how science changes its mind when the evidence finally forces it. 🌍

history.title: The Man Who Was Laughed At
history.data:
## The Man Who Was Laughed At

In 1912, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener pointed at a world map and said something that got him mocked for the rest of his life: the continents used to be joined together, and they have been drifting apart ever since.

His evidence was actually good. South America's east coast fits into Africa's west coast like puzzle pieces. Identical fossils of *Mesosaurus* show up on both continents. That reptile lived in fresh water and could never have swum an ocean. Matching rock layers and mountain ranges line up across the Atlantic. Coal sits under the ice of Antarctica, and coal forms in warm swamps. So Antarctica was not always where it is now.

Geologists still rejected it, and their reason was fair: Wegener could not explain **how**. What force could shove a continent through solid ocean floor? Without a mechanism, a good pattern is only a curiosity.

The answer arrived decades later, from the sea floor. After World War II, ships mapped the ocean bottom. They found a mountain range running down the middle of the Atlantic. Along that ridge, new rock was erupting and pushing outward. Even better, magnetic stripes frozen into that rock matched in mirror image on both sides. The sea floor was spreading.

Continents were not plowing through the ocean floor. They were riding on it.

Earth's outer shell is broken into about fifteen major **plates**. They float on the **mantle**, the hot layer of slowly flowing rock underneath.

Where plates pull apart at a **divergent** boundary, magma rises and makes new crust. That is Iceland, sitting on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and widening every year.

Where plates push together at a **convergent** boundary, one dives under the other or both crumple upward. That is the Himalayas, still growing as India presses into Asia.

Where plates grind past each other at a **transform** boundary, they stick, build stress, and snap. That is the San Andreas Fault. That snap is an earthquake.

Plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow, a few centimeters a year. Over millions of years, that is enough to build the Andes and tear open an ocean.

Wegener died on an expedition in Greenland in 1930, still dismissed. About thirty years later his idea became the foundation of modern geology.

Being right early is not the same as being believed. In science, you also have to show the mechanism.

data.instructions: Each card locks in facts from The Man Who Was Laughed At. Study the example, make it yours, and explain how it leads back to the geology.
data.sourceExcerpt: South America's east coast fits into Africa's west coast like puzzle pieces. Identical fossils show up on both continents. Matching rock layers line up across the Atlantic. Coal sits under the ice of Antarctica. Geologists rejected it because Wegener could not explain how. Plates pull apart at divergent boundaries, push together at convergent boundaries, and grind past each other at transform boundaries.

cards.target: Wegener's four kinds of evidence for continental drift
essentialFacts: Coastlines: South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces.
Fossils: identical Mesosaurus fossils on both continents, from a freshwater reptile that could not cross an ocean.
Rocks: matching rock layers and mountain ranges line up across the Atlantic.
Climate: coal under Antarctic ice means Antarctica once sat in a warm swampy place.
cards.aiExample: C-F-R-C: Coasts Fit, Rocks Connect. Coastlines, Fossils, Rocks, Climate.

Choose words that describe what each kind of evidence shows.
Say it back as a case for drift.
coachPrompts: Which of the four would a geologist have found hardest to explain any other way?

cards.target: The three boundary types and one example of each
essentialFacts: Divergent: plates pull apart, magma rises, new crust forms (the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Iceland).
Convergent: plates push together, one dives under or both crumple upward (the Himalayas).
Transform: plates grind past each other, stick, build stress, and snap in earthquakes (the San Andreas Fault).
cards.aiExample: DIVerge = DIVide (Iceland splitting). CONverge = COME together (Himalayas rising). TRANSform = TRAIN tracks sliding side by side (San Andreas).
cards.mapping: Each boundary word hides a smaller word that shows the motion: divide, come together, tracks passing. Attaching one real place to each keeps them from blurring.

scaffoldSteps: Find a hidden or sound-alike word in each boundary name.
Match a hand motion to each: pull apart, push together, slide past.
Attach one place from the lesson to each.

history.title: How We Figured It Out

data.progressionLabel: TIMELINE: A rejected idea (1912) → Accepted theory (1960s)

items.event: Mapmaker Abraham Ortelius notices that the Atlantic coastlines look like they could fit together.
Alfred Wegener proposes continental drift, using matching coastlines, fossils, rock layers, and climate clues.
Geologists reject the idea because Wegener cannot explain what force could move a continent.
Wegener dies on a Greenland expedition with his hypothesis still dismissed.
Post-war ocean mapping reveals the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a mountain range running down the ocean floor.
Harry Hess proposes sea-floor spreading: new crust forms at ridges and spreads outward.
Magnetic stripes on the sea floor are found to mirror each other on both sides of the ridge — powerful confirming evidence.
Plate tectonics is assembled from these pieces and becomes the unifying theory of modern geology.

history.meta: 8 events • how science changed its mind

items.content: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where Iceland is widening

questions.question: Why did geologists reject Wegener's continental drift for decades?
options: His fossil evidence turned out to be faked
The coastlines do not actually fit together
He could not explain what force would move the continents
He was not a trained scientist
questions.correctAnswer: He could not explain what force would move the continents

questions.question: Identical Mesosaurus fossils appear in South America and Africa. Why is that strong evidence?
options: Fossils are always found on exactly one continent
Mesosaurus was a strong ocean swimmer
The fossils are the same age as the Atlantic Ocean
Mesosaurus lived in fresh water and could not have crossed an ocean
questions.correctAnswer: Mesosaurus lived in fresh water and could not have crossed an ocean

questions.question: The Himalayas are still growing today. What kind of boundary explains that?
options: Convergent — India is pushing into Asia and both crumple upward
Divergent — the plates are pulling apart and magma fills the gap
Transform — the plates are sliding sideways past each other
None — mountains form only from volcanoes
questions.correctAnswer: Convergent — India is pushing into Asia and both crumple upward

questions.question: What finally provided the MECHANISM Wegener was missing?
options: Better maps of the continents' coastlines drawn from satellite photographs
Sea-floor spreading discovered by mapping the ocean bottom
Finding more matching fossils on land on both sides of the Atlantic
Measuring the temperature of Earth's core with deep drilling
questions.correctAnswer: Sea-floor spreading discovered by mapping the ocean bottom

questions.question: About how fast do tectonic plates move?
options: Several meters every single day, fast enough to feel
Only in sudden jumps during earthquakes, staying still between them
Around one full kilometer every year
A few centimeters a year — about as fast as fingernails grow
questions.correctAnswer: A few centimeters a year — about as fast as fingernails grow

questions.question: Coal forms in warm swamps, and coal is found under the ice of Antarctica. Explain what that tells us and why it counts as evidence.
questions.expectedAnswer: It tells us Antarctica was once in a warm, swampy climate, so it must have been located somewhere very different. It counts as evidence because coal cannot form in polar ice conditions, so the continent itself must have moved.

questions.question: The reading says 'being right early is not the same as being believed.' Explain what scientists required before accepting drift, and whether you think that standard was fair.
questions.expectedAnswer: They required a mechanism — an explanation of what force could move continents — not just matching patterns. Reasonable answers can argue either way: the standard protected science from accepting coincidences, but it also delayed a correct idea for fifty years.

reflections.text: Which piece of Wegener's evidence would have convinced you? Why that one?
Name something people believe today that you think might be overturned by future evidence.

data.question: Will the continents crash back together someday? 🌎
data.answer: Probably. Geologists model a future supercontinent forming in roughly 250 million years — it already has proposed names like Pangaea Proxima. Nobody will be around to check the prediction.

data.question: What plate am I on right now?
data.answer: Most of North America sits on the North American Plate, which extends well into the Atlantic. Parts of coastal California are on the Pacific Plate — which is why they grind past each other along the San Andreas.

data.question: Can we predict earthquakes yet?
data.answer: Not the way people want. Scientists can say which areas are at risk and roughly how often big quakes happen, but not the day or hour. Anyone claiming exact prediction is overselling.

data.question: Is Mount Everest still growing? 🏔️
data.answer: Yes, a few millimeters a year as India keeps pressing north — though erosion and earthquakes shave some of that back off.

data.question: What is the Ring of Fire?
data.answer: The horseshoe of volcanoes and earthquake zones around the Pacific, where plates converge and dive under each other. About three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes sit along it.

data.question: Was Pangaea the only supercontinent?
data.answer: No — it is just the most recent and best documented. Geologists have evidence for earlier ones like Rodinia. The continents have assembled and broken apart several times.

history.title: Explore: Reading a Coastline Like Wegener
history.meta: 6th Grade • Exploration brief • an evidence case with a mechanism check

data.title: Reading a Coastline Like Wegener
data.instructions: Build the strongest evidence case you can that two coastlines were once joined, then do what Wegener could not: say what would have to be true about the sea floor between them for the case to hold.
data.fitReason: The lesson is about how evidence and mechanism together make a scientific case. An exploration lets students assemble both halves for a real pair of coasts.

brief.context: Your class has a world map, a plate-boundary map, a list of where the same fossils and rock types are found, and a map of the age of the ocean floor (youngest rock along the mid-ocean ridges, oldest near the continents).
brief.audience: A skeptical panel of classmates playing the 1920s geologists
brief.drivingQuestion: For one pair of coastlines that look like they fit, what evidence shows they were once joined, and what does the ocean floor between them have to look like if that is true?
brief.seedDirection: Start with the coast shapes, but do not stop there: Wegener had shapes too, and he lost the argument.
lockedLessonFacts: Wegener's evidence: matching coastlines, identical fossils, matching rock layers, and climate clues such as coal under Antarctic ice.
Geologists rejected drift because no one could explain what force moves a continent.
At divergent boundaries, magma rises at a ridge and makes new crust that spreads outward.
Magnetic stripes in sea-floor rock mirror each other on both sides of the ridge.
Continents ride on plates; they do not plow through the ocean floor.
openQuestions: Where is the ridge between your two coasts, and is the youngest sea floor along it?
Do the rock types on each coast actually match, or only the shapes?
If the coasts have been moving apart for millions of years, how far apart should they be now at a few centimeters per year?
stakeholders: Future students who will use your case as a model
The scientists whose evidence you are reusing
criteria: The case uses at least three different kinds of evidence, not only coastline shape
It names the mechanism and points to a feature on the ocean-floor map that shows it
Each piece of evidence is labeled as strong, supportive, or weak
Uses at least four glossary words correctly
constraints: Only maps and data your class actually has
The panel may ask 'how do you know?' about any claim, so every claim needs a source line
Two pages including the annotated map
brief.deliverable: An annotated map of your two coastlines with the evidence marked on it, plus a one-page written case that ends with the mechanism: what the sea floor between the coasts must be doing.

parallelExample.context: A student noticed that the Red Sea looks like a crack opening between Africa and Arabia.
parallelExample.move: Instead of just pointing at the shape, she found the ridge running down the middle of the Red Sea, checked that the sea floor was youngest there, and measured that the shores are still moving apart about a centimeter a year. Shape plus ridge plus rate made a case the class could not knock down.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It shows the upgrade from Wegener's pattern to a full case: the shape is the question, the ridge is the mechanism, and the rate is the check.

supports.frameStarter: These coasts were once joined because ____, ____, and ____. The mechanism is ____, which we can see in ____.
frameChoices: Match the coastline shapes and check rock types on each side
Trace a fossil found on both coasts and ask whether it could have crossed an ocean
Find the ridge and the youngest sea floor between the coasts
Estimate how long the separation took at a few centimeters per year
coachPrompts: Which of your evidence types would Wegener have had, and which one only arrived after 1947?
If the panel says 'coincidence,' which evidence answers them?
Does your mechanism explain the direction the coasts moved?

data.coachHint: Wegener had the what. Your case needs the how. Find the ridge.
